stubs.angle: A catch block rethrows with throw; the try has a finally that prints, and an outer catch prints too: what is the console output order?
stubs.answerHinge: The finally block runs when control leaves the try statement even if the exception escapes from the catch block, so it prints after the catch body and before the outer handler.

stubs.angle: An exception is captured with ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture in a catch block and thrown later outside it; does the caller's StackTrace still contain the original throwing method?
stubs.answerHinge: ExceptionDispatchInfo.Throw restores the captured stack trace and appends the rethrow point instead of resetting it, so the original frame is kept and the output is True.

stubs.angle: A catch clause throws a new ArgumentException and the same try statement has a later catch (ArgumentException) clause; which handler prints?
stubs.answerHinge: Catch clauses of one try statement only guard the try block, so an exception thrown inside one catch clause skips its sibling clauses and is caught by the enclosing try.

stubs.angle: Three exceptions are chained through innerException; what does printing ex.GetBaseException().Message and ex.InnerException.Message give?
stubs.answerHinge: GetBaseException walks the InnerException chain to the innermost exception, while InnerException returns only the next level down.

stubs.angle: A custom OrderException constructor takes a message but the log shows the default text "Exception of type 'OrderException' was thrown."; find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: The constructor does not chain to base(message), so Exception.Message falls back to the default text and the caller's message is lost.

stubs.angle: An API parses user input that is invalid in a large share of calls on a hot path; which API shape do the .NET design guidelines recommend?
stubs.answerHinge: For failures that are common in normal use the guidelines recommend the Try-Parse pattern (bool return plus out value) alongside the throwing method, because exceptions are costly and not meant for regular control flow.

stubs.angle: A when filter itself throws a NullReferenceException while being evaluated, and a later catch clause matches the original exception; what does the program print?
stubs.answerHinge: An exception thrown during filter evaluation is swallowed and the filter counts as false, so the search continues to the next clause with the original exception.

stubs.angle: An iterator method with yield return inside try/finally is consumed by a foreach that breaks after the first item; when, if at all, does the finally print?
stubs.answerHinge: Breaking out of foreach calls Dispose on the enumerator, and Dispose runs the pending finally blocks of the iterator, so finally prints before the code after the loop.

stubs.angle: A static constructor throws InvalidOperationException and the type is accessed twice in separate try blocks while counting constructor runs; what types are caught and how many times did the constructor run?
stubs.answerHinge: A failing static constructor surfaces as TypeInitializationException wrapping the original, runs only once, and every later access rethrows the same TypeInitializationException for the lifetime of the process.

stubs.angle: A Transfer method debits one account, then calls a validation that throws for the target account; the caller catches and prints the total balance, which has shrunk; find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: The state change happens before the operation that can throw, so the exception leaves the objects half-updated; validation must run first (or changes must be rolled back) to keep the strong exception guarantee.

stubs.angle: Which set of constructors should a new custom exception type declare in a .NET 8 or later library?
stubs.answerHinge: Declare the parameterless, (string message) and (string message, Exception innerException) constructors; the legacy serialization constructor taking SerializationInfo and StreamingContext is obsolete since .NET 8 (SYSLIB0051) and should not be added.

stubs.angle: A team wants to log every exception in a service via AppDomain.FirstChanceException; which statements about this event are true?
stubs.answerHinge: The event fires for every thrown exception before any handler search, including exceptions that are later caught, and the handler can only observe, not handle or suppress, the exception.

stubs.angle: Half the team wants to replace exceptions with a Result type for all business failures; how do you decide the policy and roll it out?
stubs.answerHinge: Exceptions stay for unexpected and programming failures, while expected, frequent business outcomes become explicit return values; the line is drawn by whether the caller is expected to handle the case, applied consistently per layer rather than as a blanket rewrite.

stubs.angle: Your team ships a shared NuGet library used by other teams; which change to the exceptions a public method throws is non-breaking in a minor version?
stubs.answerHinge: Throwing a more derived exception than the one already documented is allowed, because existing catch blocks still match; throwing a new unrelated exception type is a breaking change.

stubs.angle: Production stack traces have no file names or line numbers; which build and release practices fix that and keep dumps debuggable?
stubs.answerHinge: Line numbers appear only when matching PDBs are available at runtime (deployed next to the assembly or embedded with DebugType embedded), and archiving symbols with Source Link lets later dumps map to the exact commit.

stubs.angle: Across a fleet of .NET worker services, should an unexpected exception in a background loop be caught and the loop continued, or should the process crash, and what must the platform provide for that choice?
stubs.answerHinge: After an unexpected exception the process state may be inconsistent, so the default since .NET 6 is that an unhandled BackgroundService exception stops the host, and letting it crash is safe only when an orchestrator restarts it and the work is idempotent and resumable, while catch-all loops keep broken processes alive silently.

stubs.angle: How do you design crash dump collection and analysis for hundreds of .NET service instances across clusters for years to come?
stubs.answerHinge: Dumps are enabled by runtime configuration on every instance, shipped to central restricted storage with retention and PII controls, and paired with archived symbols so automated triage can group crashes by stack signature.
